SERIALIZERS WITH FUNCTION-BASED VIEWS

In real applications, serializers are normally preferable to manually
processing large amounts of request data.

For example:

@api_view(["POST"])
def course_create(request):

    serializer = CourseSerializer(
        data=request.data
    )

    if serializer.is_valid():
        serializer.save()

        return Response(
            serializer.data,
            status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED,
        )

    return Response(
        serializer.errors,
        status=status.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST,
    )

This combines serializers with function-based views.

GET AND POST IN ONE VIEW

A single function can handle different operations:

@api_view(["GET", "POST"])
def course_list(request):

    if request.method == "GET":
        ...

    elif request.method == "POST":
        ...

This can be appropriate for simple endpoints, although larger APIs may use
more specialized views.

URL ROUTING

The function-based API view is connected to a URL like a normal Django view.

Example:

from django.urls import path
from .api_views import course_list

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "courses/",
        course_list,
        name="api-course-list",
    ),
]

Unlike APIView, the function itself is passed to path() because
@api_view has already converted it into an API view callable.

URL PARAMETERS

A function-based API view can receive URL parameters.

Example:

@api_view(["GET"])
def course_detail(request, course_id):
    ...

URL configuration:

path(
    "courses/<int:course_id>/",
    course_detail,
    name="api-course-detail",
)

A request to:

/api/courses/5/

passes:

course_id = 5

QUERY PARAMETERS

Function-based API views can inspect query parameters:

level = request.query_params.get(
    "level"
)

For example:

/api/courses/?level=beginner

The view can use the value to filter its response.

AUTHENTICATION

Function-based API views can enforce authentication with DRF permissions.

For example:

from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from rest_framework.decorators import (
    api_view,
    permission_classes,
)

@api_view(["GET"])
@permission_classes([IsAuthenticated])
def progress(request):
    ...

This requires an authenticated caller.

PUBLIC AND PROTECTED VIEWS

A course catalogue may be public:

@api_view(["GET"])
def course_list(request):
    ...

A personal progress endpoint may require authentication:

@api_view(["GET"])
@permission_classes([IsAuthenticated])
def course_progress(request):
    ...

The authorization requirement should match the sensitivity of the data.

ERROR RESPONSES

Function-based views should return useful status codes and messages.

For example:

return Response(
    {"detail": "Course not found."},
    status=status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND,
)

This gives the client a predictable response.

VALIDATION

Although a view can manually validate input, serializers are usually a
better choice when an endpoint handles structured data.

For example:

serializer = CourseSerializer(
    data=request.data
)

if not serializer.is_valid():
    return Response(
        serializer.errors,
        status=status.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST,
    )

This keeps validation logic in the serializer rather than allowing the view
to become unnecessarily large.

OBJECT RETRIEVAL

A function-based view can retrieve an object and handle missing records.

For example:

from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404

course = get_object_or_404(
    Course,
    id=course_id,
)

This produces a standard not-found response when the object does not exist
when used in the appropriate request-processing context.

FUNCTION-BASED VIEWS AND STATUS CODES

A useful pattern is:

Success:
return Response(data)

Created:
return Response(
    data,
    status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED,
)

Invalid input:
return Response(
    errors,
    status=status.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST,
)

Not found:
return Response(
    {"detail": "Not found."},
    status=status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND,
)

Unauthorized or forbidden access should be handled through appropriate
authentication and permission behavior.

API DESIGN

Function-based views should still follow clear API conventions.

For example:

GET /api/courses/
    retrieve courses

POST /api/courses/
    create a course

GET /api/courses/5/
    retrieve course 5

The HTTP method communicates the intended operation.

FUNCTION-BASED VIEWS VS APIVIEW

Function-based views:

@api_view(["GET"])
def course_list(request):
    ...

Class-based API views:

class CourseListAPIView(APIView):
    def get(self, request):
        ...

Both can implement API endpoints.

Function-based views are often convenient for small or simple endpoints.

APIView becomes useful when organizing logic into class methods and applying
class-level configuration.

TESTING FUNCTION-BASED API VIEWS

API tests should verify things such as:

- URL routing;
- allowed methods;
- response status codes;
- response data;
- authentication requirements;
- validation;
- database behavior.

For example, a test can request a public endpoint and verify:

response.status_code == 200

Another test can submit invalid data and expect:

response.status_code == 400

FUNCTION-BASED VIEWS IN THIS PROJECT

The learning platform can use function-based views for simple API operations
while keeping more complex endpoints organized through other DRF view
patterns.

The important workflow remains:

Client
  ↓
API URL
  ↓
@api_view function
  ↓
Authentication / permissions
  ↓
Serializer or application logic
  ↓
Database
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Client

KEY IDEAS

Remember:

- @api_view turns a function into a DRF API view.
- The decorator can restrict allowed HTTP methods.
- request.data contains parsed request body data.
- request.query_params contains URL query parameters.
- Response returns API data.
- status constants make response codes readable.
- @permission_classes can apply DRF permissions.
- Serializers are useful for validation and structured API input.
- Function-based views can support GET, POST, and other HTTP methods.
- URL parameters are passed directly to the function.
- Clear status codes and predictable responses improve API design.
- Automated tests should verify important API behavior.

Function-based API views provide a straightforward introduction to building
DRF endpoints and create a bridge between simple Django views and the more
structured class-based and ViewSet approaches covered later in the course.

fields.title: Class-Based API Views and Generic Views
fields.content:
Django REST Framework supports class-based views that organize API behavior
into methods and reusable classes.

Class-based views become especially useful as APIs grow beyond simple
function-based endpoints.

APIView

APIView is a core DRF class-based view.

Example:

from rest_framework.views import APIView
from rest_framework.response import Response

class CourseListAPIView(APIView):

    def get(self, request):
        return Response({
            "message": "Course list"
        })

The HTTP method is represented by a class method such as:

get()
post()
put()
patch()
delete()

The URL connects to the class using:

path(
    "courses/",
    CourseListAPIView.as_view(),
)

APIView AND FUNCTION-BASED VIEWS

A function-based view might use:

@api_view(["GET"])
def course_list(request):
    ...

An APIView might use:

class CourseListAPIView(APIView):

    def get(self, request):
        ...

Both approaches can implement APIs.

Class-based views become useful when several methods, permissions,
authentication settings, or reusable behaviors need to be organized clearly.

CLASS ATTRIBUTES

DRF class-based views can define configuration on the class.

For example:

class CourseListAPIView(APIView):
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

    def get(self, request):
        ...

This applies the specified permission behavior to the view.

HANDLING POST REQUESTS

An APIView can implement POST:

class CourseListAPIView(APIView):

    def post(self, request):
        serializer = CourseSerializer(
            data=request.data
        )

        if serializer.is_valid():
            serializer.save()

            return Response(
                serializer.data,
                status=201,
            )

        return Response(
            serializer.errors,
            status=400,
        )

This combines an APIView with a serializer.

REQUEST DATA

Class-based DRF views access request information through:

request.data
request.query_params
request.user
request.method

The same request concepts used by function-based API views apply here.

LOOKING UP OBJECTS

A detail view commonly retrieves one object.

For example:

from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404

class CourseDetailAPIView(APIView):

    def get(self, request, course_id):
        course = get_object_or_404(
            Course,
            id=course_id,
        )

        return Response(
            {
                "id": course.id,
                "title": course.title,
            }
        )

This gives a clear pattern for retrieving a single resource.

GENERIC API VIEWS

DRF provides generic class-based views for common API operations.

Examples include:

ListAPIView
CreateAPIView
RetrieveAPIView
UpdateAPIView
DestroyAPIView
ListCreateAPIView
RetrieveUpdateAPIView
RetrieveDestroyAPIView
RetrieveUpdateDestroyAPIView

These generic views reduce repeated code for common patterns.

LISTAPIVIEW

ListAPIView is designed for listing objects.

Example:

from rest_framework.generics import ListAPIView

class CourseListAPIView(ListAPIView):
    queryset = Course.objects.all()
    serializer_class = CourseSerializer

The generic view handles much of the standard GET-list behavior.

CREATEAPIVIEW

CreateAPIView is designed for creating objects.

Example:

from rest_framework.generics import CreateAPIView

class CourseCreateAPIView(CreateAPIView):
    queryset = Course.objects.all()
    serializer_class = CourseSerializer

The serializer handles validation and object creation.

RETRIEVEAPIVIEW

RetrieveAPIView is designed for retrieving one object.

Example:

from rest_framework.generics import RetrieveAPIView

class CourseDetailAPIView(RetrieveAPIView):
    queryset = Course.objects.all()
    serializer_class = CourseSerializer

The view handles the normal retrieve operation.

RETRIEVEUPDATEAPIVIEW

RetrieveUpdateAPIView supports retrieving and updating a single object.

A client can use GET to retrieve and PUT or PATCH to update, depending on the
configuration and request.

RETRIEVEUPDATEDESTROYAPIVIEW

RetrieveUpdateDestroyAPIView can support:

GET
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

for a single resource.

This is useful for endpoints that need the complete set of common
single-object operations.

QUERYSET

Generic views normally use a queryset.

Example:

queryset = Course.objects.all()

The queryset determines which records the view can work with.

A queryset can also be filtered or customized.

SERIALIZER_CLASS

Generic views generally use serializer_class:

serializer_class = CourseSerializer

The serializer controls how data is represented and validated.

URL PARAMETERS

Generic detail views can use URL parameters.

For example:

path(
    "courses/<int:pk>/",
    CourseDetailAPIView.as_view(),
)

The standard generic view can use the primary-key value to locate the object.

LOOKUP FIELD

A generic view can customize the lookup field.

For example:

lookup_field = "slug"

Then a URL might use:

path(
    "courses/<slug:slug>/",
    CourseDetailAPIView.as_view(),
)

This is useful when the API identifies resources using slugs rather than
integer IDs.

CUSTOM QUERYSET

A view can customize the queryset method:

def get_queryset(self):
    return Course.objects.filter(
        is_published=True
    )

This allows the API to apply request-specific or application-specific
filtering.

AUTHENTICATION AND PERMISSIONS

Class-based and generic views support DRF authentication and permissions.

Example:

from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated

class ProgressAPIView(ListAPIView):
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

This ensures the endpoint requires an authenticated request.

Different endpoints can have different authorization requirements.

OVERRIDING METHODS

Generic views provide reusable behavior, but developers can customize parts
of that behavior.

For example:

def perform_create(self, serializer):
    serializer.save(
        instructor=self.request.user
    )

This is useful when information should come from the authenticated user
rather than from client input.

PERFORM_UPDATE

Update behavior can also be customized:

def perform_update(self, serializer):
    serializer.save(
        updated_by=self.request.user
    )

This can help enforce application-specific rules.

PERFORM_DESTROY

Delete behavior may also be customized when an application needs additional
checks or cleanup.

GENERIC VIEWS AND SERIALIZERS

Generic views work closely with serializers.

The typical flow is:

HTTP request
  ↓
Generic view
  ↓
Serializer
  ↓
Validation
  ↓
Database operation
  ↓
Serialized response

This allows generic views to handle common API operations without repeating
the same boilerplate code.

LIST AND CREATE

ListCreateAPIView combines listing and creation.

Example:

from rest_framework.generics import ListCreateAPIView

class CourseListCreateAPIView(ListCreateAPIView):
    queryset = Course.objects.all()
    serializer_class = CourseSerializer

It can support:

GET
POST

RETRIEVE AND UPDATE

RetrieveUpdateAPIView combines:

GET
PUT
PATCH

for one resource.

RETRIEVE, UPDATE, AND DELETE

RetrieveUpdateDestroyAPIView combines:

GET
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

for one resource.

WHEN TO USE APIVIEW

APIView is useful when an endpoint has custom behavior or when the request
flow does not fit neatly into the standard generic operations.

For example, a progress endpoint might calculate data from several sources
rather than simply returning one model instance.

WHEN TO USE GENERIC VIEWS

Generic views are useful when the endpoint follows a common CRUD pattern.

For example:

GET /api/courses/
POST /api/courses/
GET /api/courses/1/
PATCH /api/courses/1/
DELETE /api/courses/1/

These operations can often be implemented with generic views and serializers
with relatively little custom code.

APIView VS GENERIC VIEW

APIView gives more direct control.

Generic views provide more reusable behavior.

A useful progression is:

Function-based API view
        ↓
APIView
        ↓
Generic API view
        ↓
ViewSet / Router

This progression helps developers choose the appropriate level of abstraction.

API DESIGN

The goal is not to use the most advanced abstraction everywhere.

Use the simplest approach that keeps the API:

- clear;
- maintainable;
- secure;
- testable;
- consistent.

DRF IN THIS PROJECT

The learning platform already contains API endpoints for course information
and authenticated course progress.

A progress endpoint may use APIView or another custom class because progress
is calculated from several related records rather than simply returning one
database object.

Other future CRUD-style endpoints may be good candidates for generic views.

TESTING CLASS-BASED AND GENERIC VIEWS

Tests should verify:

- URL routing;
- supported HTTP methods;
- response status codes;
- serializer output;
- validation;
- authentication;
- permissions;
- object lookup;
- create/update/delete behavior.

This ensures that reusable abstractions do not change the API contract
unexpectedly.

KEY IDEAS

Remember:

- APIView is a core DRF class-based API view.
- HTTP methods are implemented as class methods.
- as_view() connects class-based views to URLs.
- Generic views provide reusable implementations for common operations.
- queryset defines the records a view can access.
- serializer_class defines how data is serialized and validated.
- lookup_field can customize object lookup.
- get_queryset() can provide customized query behavior.
- perform_create(), perform_update(), and perform_destroy() can customize
  object operations.
- ListAPIView handles listing.
- CreateAPIView handles creation.
- RetrieveAPIView handles retrieval.
- ListCreateAPIView combines listing and creation.
- RetrieveUpdateDestroyAPIView combines retrieval, updating, and deletion.

Understanding APIView and generic views prepares you for ViewSets and routers,
where common API patterns can be expressed even more compactly.

fields.title: ViewSets and Routers
fields.content:
Django REST Framework provides ViewSets and routers for organizing related
API operations in a compact and consistent way.

ViewSets are especially useful when an API exposes several standard
operations for the same resource.

VIEWSETS

A ViewSet groups related API actions into a single class.

Instead of separately defining:

- list view;
- create view;
- retrieve view;
- update view;
- delete view;

a ViewSet can organize these operations together.

A basic ViewSet example is:

from rest_framework.viewsets import ViewSet
from rest_framework.response import Response

class CourseViewSet(ViewSet):

    def list(self, request):
        return Response({
            "message": "Course list"
        })

    def retrieve(self, request, pk=None):
        return Response({
            "id": pk
        })

STANDARD VIEWSET ACTIONS

Common ViewSet actions include:

list
create
retrieve
update
partial_update
destroy

These actions correspond broadly to common REST operations.

list():
Returns a collection of resources.

create():
Creates a new resource.

retrieve():
Returns one resource.

update():
Replaces an existing resource.

partial_update():
Partially updates an existing resource.

destroy():
Deletes a resource.

ROUTERS

Routers automatically generate URL patterns for ViewSets.

For example:

from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter

router = DefaultRouter()

router.register(
    "courses",
    CourseViewSet,
    basename="course",
)

urlpatterns = router.urls

The router can generate routes such as:

/courses/
/courses/{lookup}/

and map HTTP methods to ViewSet actions.

WHY ROUTERS ARE USEFUL

Without a router, developers have to write URL patterns for each operation.

Routers reduce this repeated configuration and make resource URLs more
consistent.

REGISTERING A VIEWSET

A ViewSet is commonly registered with:

router.register(
    "courses",
    CourseViewSet,
    basename="course",
)

The first argument is the URL prefix.

The second is the ViewSet class.

The basename is used when generating route names when the ViewSet does not
provide a queryset.

MODELVIEWSET

DRF provides ModelViewSet for standard CRUD-style operations.

Example:

from rest_framework.viewsets import ModelViewSet

class CourseViewSet(ModelViewSet):
    queryset = Course.objects.all()
    serializer_class = CourseSerializer

ModelViewSet provides implementations for common actions such as:

list
create
retrieve
update
partial_update
destroy

This can significantly reduce API boilerplate.

MODELVIEWSET AND ROUTER

A typical setup is:

from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter

router = DefaultRouter()

router.register(
    "courses",
    CourseViewSet,
    basename="course",
)

Then the application's URLs include:

urlpatterns = router.urls

The router creates the resource routes automatically.

CRUD MAPPING

A typical ModelViewSet maps operations like this:

GET collection
    → list()

POST collection
    → create()

GET detail
    → retrieve()

PUT detail
    → update()

PATCH detail
    → partial_update()

DELETE detail
    → destroy()

This creates a predictable REST structure.

SERIALIZERS AND MODELVIEWSET

A ModelViewSet normally works closely with a serializer.

Example:

class CourseViewSet(ModelViewSet):
    queryset = Course.objects.all()
    serializer_class = CourseSerializer

The serializer defines how Course objects are represented and validated.

QUERYSET

The queryset determines the set of objects available to the ViewSet.

Example:

queryset = Course.objects.all()

A ViewSet can also define get_queryset():

def get_queryset(self):
    return Course.objects.filter(
        instructor=self.request.user
    )

This can be useful when returned objects depend on the authenticated user.

AUTHENTICATION AND PERMISSIONS

ViewSets support DRF permissions.

For example:

from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated

class CourseViewSet(ModelViewSet):
    queryset = Course.objects.all()
    serializer_class = CourseSerializer
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

This can require authentication for the entire ViewSet.

DIFFERENT PERMISSIONS FOR DIFFERENT ACTIONS

An application may need different permissions for different operations.

For example, browsing courses could be public while creating a course
could require instructor permissions.

Action-aware permission logic can be used when necessary.

LOOKUP FIELD

ViewSets commonly use a primary key for detail lookup.

A ViewSet can instead use another field:

lookup_field = "slug"

Then a route can identify a course with:

/courses/python-programming/

This can make resource URLs more readable.

CUSTOM ACTIONS

DRF supports custom ViewSet actions with the @action decorator.

Example:

from rest_framework.decorators import action

class CourseViewSet(ModelViewSet):

    @action(
        detail=True,
        methods=["get"],
    )
    def progress(self, request, pk=None):
        ...

This can create a custom endpoint for an action that does not fit standard
CRUD operations.

DETAIL ACTIONS

When:

detail=True

the custom action applies to one resource.

For example:

/courses/5/progress/

The action receives the resource lookup value.

COLLECTION ACTIONS

When:

detail=False

the action applies to the collection.

Example:

@action(
    detail=False,
    methods=["get"],
)
def featured(self, request):
    ...

This might produce a route such as:

/courses/featured/

URL NAMES

Routers generate route names automatically based on the registered
ViewSet and basename.

This reduces the amount of manual URL configuration required.

NESTED RESOURCES

Routers do not automatically solve every possible nested-resource design.

For example:

/courses/1/lessons/

may require additional routing design depending on the application's
requirements.

Developers should choose URL structures that remain clear and predictable.

VIEWSET VS APIVIEW

APIView gives direct control over HTTP methods:

get()
post()
put()
patch()
delete()

ViewSet organizes operations into resource-oriented actions:

list()
create()
retrieve()
update()
partial_update()
destroy()

Both can be appropriate.

ViewSets become particularly useful when a resource follows standard CRUD
patterns.

MODELVIEWSET VS GENERIC VIEWS

Generic views expose individual operation patterns such as:

ListAPIView
CreateAPIView
RetrieveAPIView
UpdateAPIView
DestroyAPIView

ModelViewSet combines many common operations into one class.

A useful progression is:

Function-based view
  ↓
APIView
  ↓
Generic API view
  ↓
ViewSet
  ↓
ModelViewSet + Router

The correct choice depends on how much standard behavior the endpoint needs.

OVERRIDING VIEWSET METHODS

A ViewSet can override standard actions or helper methods when custom logic
is needed.

For example:

def perform_create(self, serializer):
    serializer.save(
        instructor=self.request.user
    )

This can associate a newly created record with the authenticated user.

CUSTOM CREATE LOGIC

A developer can override create() when the entire response or request flow
needs customization.

However, helper methods such as perform_create() are often sufficient when
only the save behavior needs to change.

CUSTOM RESPONSE BEHAVIOR

A ViewSet can return custom responses when appropriate:

return Response(
    serializer.data,
    status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED,
)

The API should still follow predictable HTTP semantics.

SECURITY

ViewSets must still enforce authentication and authorization.

Using a router does not automatically make an endpoint secure.

Important practices include:

- configure authentication;
- apply permissions;
- restrict querysets;
- verify object ownership;
- validate input through serializers;
- avoid exposing sensitive fields.

VIEWSETS IN AN LMS

A learning platform could expose resources such as:

CourseViewSet
LessonViewSet
ActivityViewSet
SubmissionViewSet
NotificationViewSet

For example:

/api/courses/
/api/courses/1/
/api/courses/1/progress/

A custom action can be useful for non-CRUD behavior such as progress.

A standard CourseViewSet might handle CRUD operations while a custom
progress action handles calculated course progress.

ROUTER-BASED API DESIGN

A typical structure is:

Client
  ↓
Router
  ↓
ViewSet action
  ↓
Authentication / permissions
  ↓
Serializer
  ↓
Database
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Client

This can provide a compact API architecture while preserving predictable
resource-oriented URLs.

WHEN NOT TO USE A VIEWSET

ViewSets are not automatically the best solution for every endpoint.

An endpoint with highly specialized behavior may be clearer as an APIView.

For example, a progress calculation that combines many different models may
benefit from a custom APIView or specialized endpoint.

The goal is to select the abstraction that keeps the API understandable and
maintainable.

TESTING VIEWSETS AND ROUTERS

Tests should verify:

- generated routes;
- supported HTTP methods;
- list and detail behavior;
- serializer validation;
- permissions;
- authentication;
- custom actions;
- object lookup;
- response status codes.

Router-generated URLs should be tested as part of the API contract.

KEY IDEAS

Remember:

- ViewSets group related API actions.
- Standard actions include list, create, retrieve, update, partial_update,
  and destroy.
- ModelViewSet provides standard CRUD behavior for Django models.
- Routers automatically generate URL patterns for ViewSets.
- router.register() connects a ViewSet to a URL prefix.
- serializer_class controls representation and validation.
- queryset determines accessible objects.
- get_queryset() can customize which objects are returned.
- lookup_field can customize detail lookup.
- @action creates custom ViewSet endpoints.
- detail=True creates a resource-specific action.
- detail=False creates a collection-level action.
- Permissions and authentication must still be enforced.
- ViewSets are useful for standard resource-oriented APIs.

ViewSets and routers provide a powerful way to organize larger DRF APIs and
prepare you for more advanced API architecture.

fields.title: Authentication and Permissions
fields.content:
Django REST Framework provides authentication and permission tools that
control who can access an API and what they are allowed to do.

Authentication answers:

"Who is making this request?"

Permissions answer:

"Is this caller allowed to perform this operation?"

These two concepts work together but perform different jobs.

AUTHENTICATION

Authentication identifies the caller.

DRF supports several authentication mechanisms, including:

- session authentication;
- token authentication;
- other configurable authentication classes.

The authentication mechanism determines how DRF identifies the user making
the request.

PERMISSIONS

After the caller is identified, DRF permissions determine whether the request
should be allowed.

For example:

from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated

class ProgressAPIView(APIView):
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

This requires an authenticated user.

AUTHENTICATION VS PERMISSIONS

Authentication:
- identifies the caller.

Permissions:
- determine whether that caller may access the endpoint.

A request can therefore be authenticated but still forbidden from performing
a particular action.

TOKEN AUTHENTICATION

DRF supports token authentication.

A token can be associated with a user and sent with an API request.

The HTTP header commonly uses:

Authorization: Token <token>

The client sends the token so the API can identify the associated user.

In this project, token authentication is already used for authenticated API
access.

TOKEN LIFECYCLE

A token should be treated like a credential.

Important practices include:

- do not expose tokens publicly;
- do not commit tokens to source control;
- rotate compromised tokens;
- use HTTPS in production;
- protect storage of client credentials.

A leaked token may allow another party to authenticate as the associated user
until the token is invalidated.

DEFAULT AUTHENTICATION

DRF can define authentication globally:

REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    "DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES": [
        "rest_framework.authentication.TokenAuthentication",
    ],
}

This allows DRF to use token authentication across API views unless a view
overrides the configuration.

DEFAULT PERMISSIONS

Global default permissions can also be configured:

REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    "DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES": [
        "rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated",
    ],
}

This means API views require authentication by default unless they explicitly
allow anonymous access.

PUBLIC ENDPOINTS

Some endpoints should remain publicly accessible.

For example, a public course catalogue might use:

from rest_framework.permissions import AllowAny

class CourseListAPIView(APIView):
    permission_classes = [AllowAny]

This explicitly allows anonymous requests.

PROTECTED ENDPOINTS

A personal progress endpoint should normally be protected:

permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

This prevents anonymous users from accessing private progress information.

COMMON PERMISSION CLASSES

DRF provides several built-in permission classes.

AllowAny:
Allows access to any request.

IsAuthenticated:
Allows authenticated users.

IsAdminUser:
Allows staff users.

IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly:
Allows anyone to read but requires authentication for write operations.

These can be combined or extended depending on the application's needs.

PERMISSION CHECKING

A permission class can deny access before the main view logic executes.

This helps keep authorization rules separate from business logic.

Example:

class StudentProgressAPIView(APIView):
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

    def get(self, request):
        ...

The permission layer ensures authentication before the GET operation proceeds.

OBJECT-LEVEL PERMISSIONS

Some authorization rules depend on a particular object.

For example:

A student may view their own submission but not another student's submission.

A generic permission may establish that the user is authenticated, while the
view or object-level permission can establish ownership.

Example filtering:

submission = get_object_or_404(
    Submission,
    id=submission_id,
    student=request.user,
)

This restricts the lookup to records belonging to the authenticated user.

SERVER-SIDE AUTHORIZATION

Authorization must happen on the server.

Hiding a button in a frontend does not provide security because a client can
still attempt to call the URL directly.

For example, this is not sufficient:

if user.is_instructor:
    show_grade_button

The backend must independently verify whether the user is allowed to grade.

ROLE-BASED API ACCESS

A learning platform may have roles such as:

Student
Instructor
Administrator

Example permissions could be:

Student:
- browse courses;
- view enrolled content;
- submit activities;
- view personal progress.

Instructor:
- manage course content;
- review submissions;
- provide grades.

Administrator:
- manage users;
- manage system data;
- access administrative functionality.

These rules should be enforced by backend authentication and authorization
logic.

CUSTOM PERMISSIONS

Applications can define custom DRF permission classes.

Example:

from rest_framework.permissions import BasePermission

class IsInstructor(BasePermission):

    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        return (
            request.user.is_authenticated
            and request.user.is_staff
        )

A view can then use:

permission_classes = [IsInstructor]

This provides a reusable authorization rule.

HAS_PERMISSION

Django's permission system can also be used from authenticated users.

For example:

if request.user.has_perm(
    "academy.change_course"
):
    ...

This can provide finer-grained authorization than simply checking whether a
user is logged in.

GROUPS AND PERMISSIONS

Django groups allow permissions to be assigned to categories of users.

For example:

Students
Instructors
Administrators

A group can receive permissions and users in that group inherit those
permissions.

This can make authorization management easier as an application grows.

PERMISSION COMPOSITION

Multiple permission classes can be used when appropriate.

Applications should choose permission behavior that matches the sensitivity
of the endpoint.

For example, a private endpoint might require authentication, while an
administrative endpoint might require both authentication and an elevated
role.

AUTHENTICATION IN API REQUESTS

A typical authenticated API request is:

Client
  ↓
Authorization header
  ↓
Authentication class
  ↓
Authenticated user
  ↓
Permission check
  ↓
API view
  ↓
Response

If authentication fails, the request should not be treated as coming from a
trusted authenticated user.

If authentication succeeds but permissions deny access, the API should return
the appropriate denial response.

401 VS 403

These status codes are related to access control but have different meanings.

401 Unauthorized is commonly used when authentication is required or the
provided credentials are not valid.

403 Forbidden means the request is understood but the authenticated caller
does not have permission to perform the operation.

The exact response behavior can depend on the authentication mechanism and
configuration.

PROTECTED PROGRESS API

The learning platform provides an authenticated progress endpoint.

Conceptually:

GET /api/courses/python-programming/progress/

should identify the caller and return progress for that authenticated student.

The important rule is that one student must not be able to request another
student's private progress simply by changing a URL value.

AUTHENTICATED USER SCOPE

An endpoint should use the authenticated user when determining private data.

For example:

student = request.user

Then queries should be restricted to the appropriate user.

This is safer than trusting a client-provided student identifier.

INSTRUCTOR VS STUDENT ACCESS

Consider a grading endpoint.

A student should not be able to modify another student's score simply by
sending a POST request to the grading URL.

The backend should verify the caller's role or permission before allowing the
operation.

API SECURITY PRINCIPLES

Important practices include:

- authenticate protected endpoints;
- enforce authorization server-side;
- restrict private data to the correct user;
- validate incoming request data;
- use HTTPS in production;
- protect API tokens;
- rotate compromised credentials;
- avoid exposing sensitive information;
- apply rate limiting where appropriate;
- test both allowed and denied access.

TESTING AUTHENTICATION AND PERMISSIONS

API tests should verify:

- anonymous access to public endpoints;
- anonymous rejection from protected endpoints;
- authenticated access to private endpoints;
- role-based restrictions;
- ownership restrictions;
- invalid or expired credentials;
- correct response status codes.

For example:

A public course endpoint should return 200 to an anonymous client.

A protected progress endpoint should reject an anonymous client.

An authenticated student should receive only their own progress.

An instructor-only endpoint should reject unauthorized students.

DRF AUTHENTICATION IN THIS PROJECT

This project already uses token authentication for API access and has a
protected course-progress endpoint.

That gives the application a concrete example of the concepts in this lesson:

Client
  ↓
Token
  ↓
DRF authentication
  ↓
Authenticated student
  ↓
Permission check
  ↓
Progress calculation
  ↓
API response

This is the same security model future API endpoints should follow.

AUTHENTICATION AND BROWSER SESSIONS

DRF token authentication is commonly used by API clients.

Django's normal web interface can use session authentication.

The two mechanisms can coexist in the same Django project.

For example:

Browser:
session authentication

Mobile client:
token authentication

The correct mechanism depends on the client and security requirements.

LEAST PRIVILEGE

A useful security principle is least privilege.

Users should receive only the access necessary to perform their tasks.

For example:

A student should not need administrative permissions.

An instructor should not automatically receive every system-management
permission.

An administrator may require broader access.

SECURE ERROR RESPONSES

Authorization failures should not reveal unnecessary sensitive information.

For example, an endpoint should not expose internal database details merely
because a user is unauthorized.

Consistent error responses make APIs easier and safer to consume.

KEY IDEAS

Remember:

- Authentication identifies the caller.
- Permissions determine what the caller can do.
- TokenAuthentication can authenticate API requests with tokens.
- IsAuthenticated protects endpoints from anonymous access.
- AllowAny can explicitly expose a public endpoint.
- IsAdminUser can restrict access to staff users.
- Custom permission classes can implement application-specific rules.
- Object-level ownership checks protect private records.
- Server-side authorization is essential.
- 401 and 403 represent different access-control situations.
- Tokens are credentials and must be protected.
- Tests should verify both permitted and denied requests.

Authentication and permissions are essential for production API design because
a functioning endpoint is not enough: the API must also ensure that the
right caller can access the right data and perform only the operations they
are authorized to perform.

fields.title: API Testing and Production Practices
fields.content:
API Testing and Production Practices

A REST API should not be considered complete merely because its endpoints work in a browser or return successful responses during manual testing. A production-ready API needs automated tests, predictable status codes, validation checks, authentication coverage, safe configuration, observability, documentation, and deployment verification.

1. Why API Testing Matters

API testing verifies that endpoints behave correctly for valid requests, invalid requests, unauthenticated users, authenticated users, and unauthorized users. It also protects the project from regressions when serializers, views, models, URLs, or permissions are changed.

A strong test suite should check both successful behavior and expected failures. Examples include:

  • Public endpoints return the expected data.
  • Authenticated endpoints reject anonymous requests when appropriate.
  • Invalid input returns a validation response instead of creating bad data.
  • Missing objects return a suitable 404 response.
  • Users cannot access resources outside their permissions.
  • Successful create, update, and delete operations return the intended status codes.

2. Django REST Framework Test Tools

Django REST Framework provides testing utilities such as APIClient, APITestCase, and request authentication helpers. These tools make it possible to test API behavior without manually opening a browser.

A simple example is: 

from rest_framework.test import APITestCase

class CourseAPITests(APITestCase):
    def test_course_list(self):
        response = self.client.get("/api/courses/")
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)

The DRF API test client works with JSON requests and provides an interface similar to an actual HTTP client.

3. Testing Authentication

Authentication should be tested explicitly. A protected endpoint should reject an anonymous request and allow a properly authenticated request.

For token authentication, a test can authenticate the API client using a user token: 

from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token

token = Token.objects.create(user=user)
self.client.credentials(
    HTTP_AUTHORIZATION=f"Token {token.key}"
)

The test can then make the protected request and verify the expected status code and response body.

It is useful to test at least three cases:

  • Anonymous request.
  • Authenticated request from an ordinary user.
  • Authenticated request from a privileged user where administrator permissions matter.

4. Testing Permissions

Authentication answers the question "Who is making the request?" Permissions answer the question "Is this user allowed to perform this action?"

Permission tests should cover actions such as viewing, creating, updating, and deleting resources. They should also verify object ownership when ownership rules exist.

For example, if a user is allowed to edit only their own submission, the test suite should confirm that:

  • The owner can access or modify the submission.
  • A different authenticated user cannot modify it.
  • An anonymous user is rejected when authentication is required.

5. Testing Serializers and Validation

Serializers should be tested independently as well as through endpoint tests. Important cases include required fields, invalid values, incorrect data types, duplicate values, maximum lengths, and cross-field validation rules. 

serializer = CourseSerializer(data={
    "title": "",
    "description": "Example"
})

self.assertFalse(serializer.is_valid())
self.assertIn("title", serializer.errors)

Validation tests make failures easier to diagnose because they identify whether the problem belongs to the serializer rather than the view or URL layer.

6. HTTP Status Codes

Clients depend on predictable HTTP status codes. Common responses include:

  • 200 OK for a successful retrieval or operation.
  • 201 Created when a new resource is successfully created.
  • 204 No Content for a successful operation with no response body.
  • 400 Bad Request for invalid request data.
  • 401 Unauthorized when authentication is required but missing or invalid.
  • 403 Forbidden when the identity is known but access is not permitted.
  • 404 Not Found when the requested resource does not exist.

Tests should assert status codes as well as important response fields. This helps maintain a stable API contract for frontend applications and other clients.

7. Testing the Project Progress API

This project includes an authenticated course progress API at: 

/api/courses/<slug>/progress/

A complete test should verify that an authenticated student receives course progress data, while an unauthenticated request is rejected. The test should also cover the case where a user is authenticated but is not enrolled in the requested course.

Useful response fields include enrollment status, course completion status, overall percentage, lesson percentage, activity percentage, average score, module progress, and recent assessments.

8. Pagination

Large collection endpoints should not return unlimited amounts of data. Pagination allows an API to return manageable pages of results.

Tests should verify:

  • The response format for paginated results.
  • The number of items returned per page.
  • Navigation metadata where configured.
  • Correct behavior on later pages and empty pages.

9. Throttling and Abuse Protection

Throttling limits the frequency of requests from clients. It can help protect API resources from accidental request storms and certain forms of abuse.

When throttling is enabled, tests should confirm that normal traffic works and that requests exceeding configured limits receive the expected throttling response.

10. Logging and Observability

Production APIs need useful logs so that failures can be investigated. Logging should capture relevant events such as request failures, authentication problems, server errors, and important application actions.

Sensitive data such as passwords, raw authentication tokens, and confidential user information should never be written to logs.

11. Error Handling

Error responses should be structured and predictable. Clients should receive useful information about validation errors while internal implementation details and stack traces remain hidden in production.

Development settings may expose detailed debugging information, but production settings should disable Django debug output.

12. API Documentation

API documentation explains available endpoints, HTTP methods, parameters, authentication requirements, request formats, response formats, and possible error responses.

Good documentation allows another developer to integrate with the API without reading the application's internal implementation.

13. Secure Production Configuration

Production settings should keep secrets outside source code. Values such as secret keys, database connection strings, API credentials, and other sensitive settings should be supplied through environment variables or another secure configuration system.

Production deployments should also use appropriate values for:

  • DEBUG=False
  • Allowed hosts
  • Secure database configuration
  • HTTPS and secure cookies where applicable
  • Trusted origins and CSRF configuration where required
  • Static file handling
  • Application logging

14. Deployment Verification

A deployment is not finished when the server starts successfully. The deployed API should be tested from outside the server environment.

A practical verification sequence is:

  1. Open the application homepage.
  2. Verify public API endpoints.
  3. Authenticate with a test account.
  4. Call protected endpoints.
  5. Verify expected permissions.
  6. Check database-backed data.
  7. Review application logs for errors.

For this project, the Render deployment should be checked separately from the local development environment because production configuration, database contents, static files, and environment variables can differ.

15. API Testing Checklist

  • Test every important endpoint.
  • Test valid and invalid inputs.
  • Test anonymous and authenticated access.
  • Test permission boundaries.
  • Assert expected status codes.
  • Assert important response fields.
  • Test serializer validation.
  • Test pagination and throttling when enabled.
  • Keep secrets out of source code and logs.
  • Run the full regression suite before deployment.
  • Perform a production smoke test after deployment.

16. Practical Exercise

Create automated tests for one protected DRF endpoint in this project. Your tests should include an anonymous request, an authenticated request, an authorization failure case, and a successful response. Then run the complete Django test suite and confirm that existing functionality still passes.

Learning Outcome

After completing this lesson, you should be able to write automated API tests, verify authentication and permissions, validate response codes and data, identify production configuration requirements, and perform basic deployment verification for a Django REST Framework application.
